question: For every positive real number $x$, let $g(x)=\lim _{r \rightarrow 0}((x+1)^{r+1}-x^{r+1})^{1/r}$. What is the limit of $g(x)/x$ as $x$ goes to infinity?
model_outputs:
We have \begin{align*}
\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{g(x)}{x} &= \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\lim _{r \rightarrow 0}((x+1)^{r+1}-x^{r+1})^{1/r}}{x} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \lim _{r \rightarrow 0} \frac{(x+1)^{r+1}-x^{r+1}}{x^{1+r}} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \lim _{r \rightarrow 0} \frac{(x+1)^{r+1}-x^{r+1}}{x^{r+1}} \cdot \frac{x}{1} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \lim _{r \rightarrow 0} \frac{(x+1)^{r+1}-x^{r+1}}{x^{r+1}} \cdot \frac{x}{1} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \lim _{r \rightarrow 0} \frac{(x+1/x)^{r+1}-1}{x} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \lim _{r \rightarrow 0} \frac{(1+1/x)^{r+1}-1}{x} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\ln \left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{r+1}-\ln 1}{x} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\ln \left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{r+1}-0}{x} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{(r+1) \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)}{x} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{(r+1)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)}{x} \\
&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{r+1}{x^{2}} \\
&=0
\end{align*}The answer is (E).

question:
A tank contains 100 gal of water and $50 \mathrm{oz}$ of salt. Water containing a salt concentration of $\frac{1}{4}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right) \mathrm{oz} / \mathrm{gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $2 \mathrm{gal} / \mathrm{min}$, and the mixture in the tank flows out at the same rate.

The rate of change of the amount of salt in the tank is the rate at which salt flows into the tank minus the rate at which salt flows out. The concentration of salt in the tank is therefore
\[\frac{s(t)}{100}=\frac{1}{4}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right).\]
The rate of change of the amount of salt in the tank is
\begin{align*}
s^{\prime}(t)&=2\left[\frac{1}{4}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right)\right]\\
&\qquad-2\left[\frac{s(t)}{100}\right]\\
&=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right)-\frac{s(t)}{50}.
\end{align*} We want to find the long-time behavior of $s(t)$. This is the same as finding the steady-state solution of the differential equation
\begin{align*}
s^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right)-\frac{s(t)}{50}.
\end{align*} We can rewrite the equation above as
\begin{align*}
s^{\prime}(t)+\frac{s(t)}{50}&=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right)\\
\Rightarrow\qquad 50s^{\prime}(t)+s(t)&=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right).
\end{align*} This is a linear differential equation with constant coefficients. We solve this equation by finding an integrating factor, $\mu(t)$. We have
\begin{align*}
\mu(t)&=e^{\int\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) d t}=e^{\frac{1}{2} t}.
\end{align*} Multiplying both sides of the equation by $\mu(t)$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
50e^{\frac{1}{2} t} s^{\prime}(t)+e^{\frac{1}{2} t} s(t)&=\frac{1}{2} e^{\frac{1}{2} t}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right).
\end{align*} The left-hand side of the equation is the derivative of $e^{\frac{1}{2} t} s(t)$. We have
\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{d t}\left(e^{\frac{1}{2} t} s(t)\right)&=\frac{1}{2} e^{\frac{1}{2} t}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right).
\end{align*} Integrating both sides of this equation, we have
\begin{align*}
e^{\frac{1}{2} t} s(t)&=\int\left[\frac{1}{2} e^{\frac{1}{2} t}\left(1+\frac{1}{2} \sin t\right)\right] d t\\
&=\frac{1}{2} e^{\frac{1}{2} t}\left(t+\frac{1}{2} \cos t\right)+C.
\end{align*} We use $C$ to denote the constant of integration. We have $s(0)=50$, and so
\begin{align*}
50&=e^{0}\left(0+\frac{1}{2} \cos 0\right)+C\\
\Rightarrow\qquad C&=50-\frac{1}{2}.
\end{align*} Thus, we have
\begin{align*}
e^{\frac{1}{2} t} s(t)&=\frac{1}{2} e^{\frac{1}{2} t}\left(t+\frac{1}{2} \cos t\right)+50-\frac{1}{2}\\
\Rightarrow\qquad s(t)&=\left(t+\frac{1}{2} \cos t\right)+50-\frac{1}{2} e^{-\frac{1}{2} t}.
\end{align*} The solution $s(t)$ oscillates about the constant value $50-\frac{1}{2}=49.5$. The amplitude of the oscillation is the distance between this constant value and the value of $s(t)$ when $t=0$. This value is $s(0)=50-\frac{1}{2} \cos 0=49.5$. The distance between $49.5$ and $49.5$ is $0$. The answer is (J).
